A good way to think about an RSU vest is: it’s now compensation you’ve already received, plus an investment decision.

What to do depends on 3 things:

Taxes and withholding
RSUs are typically taxed when they vest, and some shares may already have been withheld or sold to cover taxes. Start by checking what actually landed in your brokerage and what was withheld.

Concentration risk
If keeping the shares would leave too much of your money tied to your employer, that increases single-company risk. A common question to ask is: if this same amount were cash today, would I choose to buy my employer’s stock with it? If not, selling some or all may be reasonable.

Near-term cash needs
If you need cash for taxes, debt, or upcoming expenses, that may matter more than holding the stock.

A simple framework:

Sell all if you want to reduce employer-stock risk immediately.
Sell enough to cover taxes or a planned use of the money.
Hold some/all only if you’re comfortable with the risk and it still fits your broader allocation.

Before deciding what to sell after a $42,000 Microsoft RSU vest, check these items first:
1) Confirm how much tax was withheld at vest

RSUs are generally taxed as wages at vest, not at grant, and an 83(b) election does not apply to RSUs. Employers commonly withhold federal income tax on separately identified supplemental wages at a 22% flat rate unless special higher-income rules apply. Social Security and Medicare withholding also apply through payroll. (
irs.gov
)

For a quick check on $42,000 of vested value:

Federal withholding: about $9,240 if withheld at 22%.
Social Security: 6.2% only up to the annual wage base; for 2026 the wage base is $184,500, so this may be $0 if you already exceeded it earlier this year. (
irs.gov
)
Medicare: 1.45% generally still applies, and Additional Medicare Tax can matter at higher wages. The IRS specifically notes withholding accuracy can differ when bonuses, capital gains, or Additional Medicare Tax are involved. (
irs.gov
)
Washington state: no state wage income tax, so there is normally no Washington state income-tax withholding to check.

$4,400 for self-only HDHP coverage

You must be covered by an HSA-eligible HDHP.

If you become eligible midyear, your limit may be prorated.

If either spouse has family HDHP coverage, both spouses are generally treated as having family coverage for limit-sharing purposes, and the family limit is split between you unless you agree otherwise. (

A practical way to estimate it

For each insured person, use:

Needed coverage =

Income replacement: annual amount your family would need from that person × number of years
+ debts to pay off: mortgage, car loans, credit cards, personal loans
+ one-time costs: funeral, moving, legal, emergency cushion
+ future goals: childcare, college, eldercare, other planned support
− existing assets available for survivors: savings set aside for this purpose
− existing life insurance: employer coverage + personal policies
Quick rule of thumb

A rough starting point is often 7–12× annual income, then adjust for:

higher end if you have young kids, a large mortgage, or one income is hard to replace
lower end if you have substantial savings or few dependents
A simple example

If one person earns $90,000 and you want:

10 years of support = $900,000
$250,000 mortgage payoff
$100,000 for kids’ costs / college
$25,000 final expenses
minus $150,000 existing coverage

Then estimated need is about $1.125 million.
